intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene (601906) on chromosome 12q13.

checks.evidence_quote: a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation (p.R332W) in all affected individuals but the atypical case
checks.explanation: Homozygous WNT10b mutation identified as cause of the recessive SHFM; SHFM6 is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The WNT10B gene is located on chromosome 12q13.

paragraphs.text: Split-hand/foot malformation-6 is an autosomal recessive form of split-hand/foot malformation (ectrodactyly). Affected individuals have central reductions of the feet, with or without involvement of the hands, and the malformation pattern can vary within a family (Ugur and Tolun, 2008; Gul and Oktenli, 2002). Split-hand/foot malformation in general is genetically heterogeneous. Variable expressivity, reduced penetrance, and accompanying distal limb anomalies make phenotypic classification difficult (Elliott and Evans, 2006).

checks.evidence_quote: We studied a large consanguineous kindred afflicted with autosomal recessive SHFM.

checks.claim: Individuals affected with SHFM6 have central reductions of the feet, with or without involvement of the hands.
checks.evidence_quote: Twelve affected members had central feet reductions with or without hand involvement

checks.claim: The malformation pattern of SHFM6 can vary within a family.
checks.evidence_quote: A variable intrafamilial expression of the malformation pattern is apparent.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports variable expression within the family.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation in general is genetically heterogeneous.
checks.evidence_quote: genetic heterogeneity, with at least five loci identified to date, further complicates management of affected patients and their families
checks.explanation: The abstract says SHFM is genetically heterogeneous, with at least five loci identified.

checks.claim: Variable expressivity, reduced penetrance, and accompanying distal limb anomalies make phenotypic classification of split-hand/foot malformation difficult.
checks.evidence_quote: The deficiency in SHFM patients can also be accompanied by other distal limb anomalies including polydactyly and/or syndactyly. This variability causes the phenotypic classification of SHFM to be far from straightforward
checks.explanation: The abstract names variable expressivity, reduced penetrance and accompanying distal limb anomalies, and says this variability makes phenotypic classification difficult.

paragraphs.text: Freire-Maia (1971) reported a recessive form of ectrodactyly and discussed what it means for genetic counseling. Verma et al. (1976) described affected sibships born to first-cousin parents. They concluded that their family, together with earlier reports, further showed that split-hand and split-foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Mufti and Wood (1987) observed ectrodactyly in sisters and half sisters of an extended family and concluded that an autosomal recessive gene was the likely mode of inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) questioned whether a rare autosomal recessive form of split hand/foot malformation exists. As an alternative, they proposed a 2-locus model. In this model, a dominant split hand/foot mutation is controlled by a gene at a second locus, and a dominant mutation at the controlling locus makes the split hand/foot mutation nonpenetrant. Gul and Oktenli (2002) studied an inbred kindred with 9 affected members and discussed both autosomal recessive inheritance and a 2-locus model. They noted that most familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

paragraphs.text: Ugur and Tolun (2008) used a candidate gene approach in a consanguineous kindred with autosomal recessive SHFM mapped to 12q13. They identified a homozygous missense mutation in the WNT10B gene (R332W). The mutation was present in all affected individuals except the one with atypical SHFM, and it was also present in an asymptomatic female. The authors described this as the first reported WNT10B mutation involved in the pathogenesis of limb development and the first recessive mutation in SHFM.

paragraphs.text: In an Indian girl with SHFM6, Kantaputra et al. (2018) identified a novel homozygous 3-bp deletion (c.695_697delACA) in the WNT10B gene. The deletion was predicted to remove asparagine-232 in frame (Asn232del). Protein modeling suggested that deleting this single amino acid at a critical position likely severely affects protein structure and function, probably shortening the lifetime of the protein and preventing it from binding its receptors and other ligands.
